newsitem.title: USA: Leaner inventories sap economy at close of 1996.
newsitem.headline: Leaner inventories sap economy at close of 1996.

text.p: A smaller buildup in stocks of unsold goods led to slower economic growth in the final quarter last year than previously thought, the Commerce Department said Friday.

Instead of booming ahead at a 4.7 percent annual rate, gross domestic product increased at a still-hearty 3.9 percent pace from October through December -- nearly double the 2.1 percent GDP advance posted in the third quarter last year.
Analysts said lower inventories meant the economy might get a modest boost this year from busier factories as stocks of goods are built up once more.
That prospect may not please Federal Reserve policymakers already uneasy about the possibility that rapid growth might fuel runaway prices.
"The basic message is that some of the growth we thought was behind us may well still be ahead of us," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.

Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress this week that the central bank may need to raise interest rates in coming months to quash inflation before it starts in order to keep the six-year-old expansion on track.

"The economy may be moving uncomfortably fast for them," said economist Bill Cheney of John Hancock Financial Services in Boston. "The surging stock market, relatively tight labour markets, lower inventories and strong consumer confidence could ignite inflation."

A report from Chicago purchasing managers on Friday showed a slight pickup in business activity in the Midwest during February as its Chicagoland Business Barometer rose to a seasonally adjusted 56.2 from 55.9 in January.
Any reading over 50 signals growing manufacturing activity.
Separately Friday, the National Association of Realtors said sales of existing, or used, homes increased in January by 2.1 percent to a rate of 3.94 million a year.
Relatively low mortgage rates and strong job growth were providing underpinning for the housing sector, much as lower inventories were expected to do for production rates.
"As consumers become more confident in the economy, they're more willing to make the investment in a home," said John Tuccillo, economist for the realtors' lobby group.
"This drives up demand, which drives up prices," he added.

A University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey, made available only to paying customers, showed a jump in February to an index level of 99.7 from 97.4 in January, a sign the economy may get continuing stimulus from consumer spending.

GDP, the broadest measure of national economic activity since it values all goods and services produced within U.S. borders, is forecast to slow in the current quarter to a rate around 2.5 percent a year.

When the Commerce Department made its first estimate of fourth-quarter GDP a month ago, it had to estimate December inventories. The revised figure reflected an actual sell-off of stocks in December instead of the slower growth the department assumed.
"The downward revision to real GDP was more than accounted for by the downward revision to inventory investment," the Commerce Department said.

Despite the weaker figure for fourth-quarter GDP, the revised report showed the economy had considerable momentum as last year ended. The quarterly GDP figure will be revised a final time a month from now.

For example, consumer spending -- which fuels two-thirds of national economic activity -- was revised upward modestly to show an annual rate of increase of $39.8 billion, instead of $38.8 billion as previously estimated.
Two inflation measures in the GDP report were left unchanged, reflecting a slowing pace of price changes as 1996 ended instead of higher costs.
The implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.4 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter compared with 1.7 percent in the third quarter.
The fixed-weights measure of price changes gained at a 1.8 percent rate in last year's final quarter, down from 2 percent in the third quarter.
